title: The Mandate
gateMessage: Your term ends today. Face what you have built.

narrative.text: One year. Fifty-two weeks. Three hundred and sixty-five days since you stood at the inauguration podium and promised to change Veltria. The country you inherited was a Halvekist state with democratic aspirations, an economy built for extraction rather than prosperity, a military that had never been subordinate to civilian authority, a society divided by ethnicity and class and the unhealed wounds of the Silent Clearances. The country you leave — whether through election, resignation, exile, or death — is different. Whether it is better depends on what you did with the fifty-two weeks you were given.

You will be judged. Not by historians — historians will argue about your Chancellorship for decades and reach no consensus. Not by the international community — they will remember you as convenient or inconvenient depending on their interests. You will be judged by the people who lived through your decisions: the factory worker in Kravenstal who kept or lost her job, the Dravenni family who received or were denied language rights, the soldier who came home from the war or didn't, the child who grew up under your constitution or your emergency powers. And by your own children — Liora, Tomas — who will carry what you did and what you failed to do for the rest of their lives. That is the judgment that matters. That is the judgment you cannot escape. You wouldn't want to.

choices.text:
The Constitution of the Republic of Veltria survived its first year, which is the hardest year for any constitution. The institutions you built held. The Constitutional Court established its independence through a series of rulings that surprised everyone — sometimes siding with the government, sometimes against it, always with reasoning that demonstrated the law was more than the sum of political pressures. The military remained in its barracks through an election cycle, which the old Halvekist regime had never managed. The Dravenni language was spoken openly in Dravenhollow for the first time in a generation. The economy did not boom — economies recovering from near-collapse do not boom — but it stabilized, and stabilization after crisis is its own kind of miracle.

The election was held on schedule. You either won a second term on the strength of your record, or you lost narrowly to a successor who campaigned on continuing the constitutional project while criticizing your methods. Either outcome is a victory for the democracy you built. The peaceful transfer of power — the thing that makes a republic a republic — happened in Veltria for the first time since before Halvek. You either handed over the seal of office or accepted it again, and in both cases the institutions functioned.

Jonas stayed — or didn't — but the marriage either deepened into a partnership forged by crisis or ended with the mutual respect of two people who tried something hard and learned they couldn't do it together. Liora published her first book: a history of the transitional period based in part on the papers she'd once leaked. It was fair, which meant it was critical, which meant it was the kind of accountability democracy requires. Tomas finished school — not easily, not smoothly, but he finished. He was accepted to the University of Kravenstal to study engineering. He told you, quietly, that he wanted to build things. After everything that had been destroyed, he wanted to build.

Veltria is not a utopia. It is a functioning democracy with deep problems and real divisions and a population that is learning, slowly, that self-governance is not the absence of conflict but the peaceful management of it. You gave them the tools. They are using them. That is enough. That is everything.

You kept Halvek's powers and used them well. That is the generous version. The less generous version is that you proved authoritarianism works if the authoritarian is competent. The constitution passed, but the emergency powers you retained allowed you to govern by executive order whenever the parliament resisted. The parliament resisted often, and you overrode it often, and after a while the parliament stopped resisting because resistance had become symbolic — a performance of opposition that changed no outcomes.

The economy recovered. The Tyvaren threat was managed — through strength, through diplomacy, through the credible threat of force that Vukov understood because it was the only language he spoke. The Dravenni situation stabilized, though 'stabilized' meant different things depending on whether you had embraced or suppressed them. The military stayed in its barracks, not because it believed in civilian control but because Brenner — or whoever replaced Brenner — believed in you personally. The distinction is the entire difference between a democracy and a competent dictatorship.

Your children grew up in the shadow of your authority. Liora became a journalist, but one who was careful about what she wrote — not because you threatened her, but because she understood, without being told, that certain truths about the government would harm her mother and that harming her mother was different from holding power accountable. Tomas drifted away from the Ironborn and toward a quiet life that asked nothing political of him. You protected them from the consequences of your governance by making sure there were no consequences — no scandals, no purges, no visible repression. Just the steady accumulation of executive power, justified each time by a crisis that was real enough to make the justification plausible.

The election came. You won. The opposition called it unfair. The international observers called it 'generally free but with significant structural advantages for the incumbent.' You could have retired. You didn't. You told yourself the country still needed you. You were probably right. The tragedy of the benevolent autocrat is that they are always right about what the country needs and always wrong about what the country will need after them. The system you built depends entirely on you. When you are gone — and you will be gone, eventually — there will be no system. There will only be whoever comes next. And they will have all of Halvek's powers and none of your restraint.

The war ended on a Thursday in February, when Marshal Vukov's government — depleted, isolated, facing an economic crisis of its own — accepted a ceasefire negotiated through the International Forum. The Gravenmark Pass remained Veltrian. The border was restored. The dead were buried. The living began the long work of learning to live with what they had done and what had been done to them.

Veltria emerged from the war diminished but intact. The northern infrastructure had to be rebuilt — roads, bridges, the rail line through the Korven Forest. The reconstruction became a national project, the thing that united a country that had been fracturing for fifty-two weeks. You established the War Reconstruction Authority and appointed Dusek to lead it — a military officer rebuilding civilian infrastructure, a symbol you hoped the country would understand. She accepted. She told you she was tired of destroying things. She wanted to build something. You understood.

The international community, which had offered sympathy but not soldiers during the fighting, offered reconstruction loans. You accepted them — conditionally, carefully, with terms that preserved Veltrian sovereignty. You had learned, through the long months of the war, that survival sometimes requires accepting help you don't trust from people you don't like. The principle applied to international finance as much as it applied to military alliances.

At home, the war had changed your family in ways you were still discovering. Jonas, who had spent the war organizing civilian relief in Kravenstal, had found a purpose that was separate from your governance but complementary to it. The distance between you had closed — not completely, not permanently, but genuinely. Liora had covered the war as a journalist, filing reports that were honest about both Veltrian courage and Veltrian failures. You were proud of her in a way that transcended your role as Chancellor. Tomas had volunteered at a field hospital. What he saw there aged him. It also clarified something in him — a resolve, a seriousness, a decision about the kind of person he wanted to be. He did not talk about it. He didn't need to. You could see it in the way he carried himself.

You stood at the memorial service for the eight thousand and read their names — not all of them, there were too many, but a selection meant to represent the whole. You said: 'They gave us the country. We will spend the rest of our lives earning what they gave.' The country believed you. So did you. That was not nothing. After fifty-two weeks, that was everything.

The occupation began on a grey morning in early spring, when Tyvaren forces entered Kravenstal without resistance. The army had fought until it could not fight. The government had negotiated the terms of surrender: civilian administration would continue under Veltrian officials, but all policy decisions required Tyvaren approval. You were allowed to remain as Chancellor — a figurehead, an administrator of occupation, the face of a government that had lost the war but was being permitted to manage the peace. You accepted. The alternative was a military governor and the dissolution of every institution you had built. You chose the lesser humiliation. The humiliation was still complete.

You govern now from the same office, in the same building, under the same portraits of Veltrian landscapes. But every decision you make is reviewed by a Tyvaren political officer who sits in an office two floors above yours. You have learned to govern within the space they allow you — protecting what you can, conceding what you must, waiting for the international situation to shift in ways that might loosen their grip. You do not know if that will happen in your lifetime. You do it anyway.

The family scattered. Jonas took a position at an architectural firm in Stellamere — he could not live under occupation, he said, and he could not ask you to leave. You understood. You did not ask him to stay. Liora remained in Veltria, working for an underground newspaper that the occupiers periodically shut down and that periodically reopened under a different name. You did not tell her to stop. You were proud of her in a way you could not express publicly without endangering her and the fragile arrangement that kept you in office. Tomas — Tomas was conscripted into a Tyvaren labor program for Veltrian youth. You could not prevent it. You visited him once a month. He did not blame you. The absence of blame was the worst thing you had ever experienced.

At night, alone in the residence, you read through the old briefings — the decisions you made, the battles you authorized or deferred, the moments when a different choice might have produced a different outcome. You will never know which choice it was. The counter-factuals multiply endlessly. The occupation is the reality. You govern from within it because governing is what you do — the only thing you have ever known how to do. The country survives. You survive. Whether that is victory or its absence depends on what comes next. You will not be the one who decides what comes next. You will be the one who kept the institutions intact long enough for someone else to decide.

The ceasefire held — not because either side was satisfied, but because neither side could continue. The border was redrawn. Veltria lost territory in the Gravenmark region — not the pass itself, but the approaches, the villages, the farms that had been Veltrian for three generations. Tyvaren gained less than it had demanded and more than Veltria could afford to lose. Both sides called it a victory. Both sides knew it was not.

The armistice negotiations took six months. You led the Veltrian delegation personally — you could not send someone else to give away pieces of the country you had sworn to defend. The Tyvaren foreign minister, the same Volkov who had offered you false compromises at Strevna, was cordial and precise and completely uninterested in the human reality of the border communities that were being transferred to his country's control. You negotiated the evacuation of Veltrian civilians from the ceded territories — not the territory, you could not keep the territory, but the people. Volkov conceded the evacuation. It was the only concession you won. The people of the lost villages were resettled in the south. They called themselves the Displaced. They would call themselves that for the rest of their lives.

At home, the stalemate was received as a defeat by the Iron Covenant, a relief by the business community, and a tragedy by the border families. Parliament ratified the armistice by a margin of four votes. You considered resigning. You did not resign. You had lost a war you had not started, against an enemy you had warned the world about, with allies who sent statements instead of soldiers. You had also kept Veltria sovereign. The difference between defeat and negotiated survival was a matter of perspective. You chose the perspective that allowed you to continue governing.

Jonas asked you, the night after the armistice was signed, whether you thought it was worth it. The war, the dead, the territory, the compromises. You told him you didn't know. You told him you would never know. He nodded. He did not ask again. Liora wrote an editorial calling the armistice 'the least worst outcome that was actually possible.' High praise, from her. Tomas asked if he would have to fight in the next war. You told him you hoped there wouldn't be a next war. He looked at you the way fourteen-year-olds look at adults who have just lied to them without meaning to.

Veltria survived. Smaller, poorer, more tired than it had been a year ago. But it survived. And survival, you have learned, is the foundation on which everything else is built. The next government will build. You held the foundation. That is enough. It has to be.

General Brenner rules Veltria now. The junta calls itself the 'Provisional Authority for National Stability,' a name designed to sound temporary and administrative rather than what it is: a military dictatorship that has suspended the constitution, dissolved parliament, and placed you under house arrest or driven you into exile, depending on the choices you made when the tanks came.

If you are in exile: you govern from Stellamere, broadcasting to Veltria on shortwave radio, coordinating with the loyalist remnants that Dusek has built into a genuine resistance network. The international community recognizes your government as legitimate, which means you attend diplomatic functions and issue statements that are reported in the international press. You are a Chancellor without a country. The country is still there — occupied, repressed, waiting. You tell yourself you will return. You believe it most days. The days you don't are the hardest.

If you are under house arrest: you live in the residence, monitored by junta security, permitted visitors once a week, your mail read before you receive it. Brenner visits occasionally — not to gloat, he is not a gloater, but to update you on the 'stabilization process' as though you were still a colleague whose opinion he valued. He is not cruel. He is worse than cruel: he is certain. He believes he saved the country from chaos. He may even be right about the chaos — the constitutional crisis, the factional conflicts, the economic pressures were real. But he has replaced chaos with the stillness of a country that is no longer allowed to make its own mistakes.

Your family adapted to your absence or your captivity. Jonas became the public face of the 'Free Veltria' movement in Stellamere, speaking at rallies you were not allowed to attend. Liora wrote about the junta for international publications under a pseudonym — her real name would endanger you both. Tomas grew up in a country where soldiers on street corners were normal and the radio played martial music between bulletins. He learned not to talk about politics. He learned not to talk about you. The silence protected him. It also cost him something you could see in his eyes but could not name.

The junta will not last forever. No junta does. The question is what replaces it — a restored democracy, a new strongman, a chaos worse than either. You will not be the one who decides. You will be the one who preserved the idea of legitimate governance through the years when that idea had no territory, no army, no power except the power of being remembered. Sometimes that is enough. Sometimes it is not. The historians will tell you which. You will not live to read their verdict.

The IMA program ran its course. The economy stabilized — in the technical sense that the Krone stopped falling and the bond yields stopped rising and the international accountants in Stellamere certified that Veltria had met its structural adjustment targets. In the human sense, the economy did not stabilize. It contracted, redistributed, hollowed out. The public sector shed sixty thousand jobs. The Grain Authority was sold to an Arcturian conglomerate that raised prices by thirty percent within six months. Northern Rail was acquired by investors who extracted its value and deferred its maintenance. State Broadcasting became a commercial network that aired imported programming because domestic production was too expensive. The country was solvent. The people were poorer. The IMA considered this a success.

You administered the austerity because the alternative was default. You explained this to the country in radio addresses that grew grimmer each month. You did not try to make the explanations inspiring. You had tried that, early on, and the country had seen through it. You settled for honest: this is what we must do to survive, it will hurt, I am sorry. The honesty did not make the policies more popular. It did, perhaps, make them more survivable — people can endure hardship that is acknowledged. What breaks them is hardship that is denied.

The Workers' Coalition either became your ally in resisting the worst of the IMA conditions or became your most effective opposition. Soraya Khaled either worked with you to negotiate modifications or campaigned against you as the face of international austerity. Either way, the labor movement emerged from the crisis stronger than it had been before — crisis radicalizes, and austerity provides a target. The next election, whenever it comes, will be fought on economic lines that your Chancellorship defined.

Your family paid a different kind of price. Jonas understood the economic logic but could not accept the human cost. The tension between those positions became the background radiation of your marriage. Liora wrote a series of articles about the human impact of the IMA program — detailed, devastating, impossible to refute. You read them with pride and pain in equal measure. Tomas asked you once why his classmates' parents were losing their jobs. You gave him the structural explanation. He said: 'That doesn't answer my question.' He was right.

You finished your term. You did not run again. The country you left was poorer than the country you inherited, but it was also more honest about its problems and more realistic about its options. You had governed through an economic crisis not of your making with tools that were inadequate to the task. The judgment of history will depend on whether the stabilization held long enough for growth to resume. You will not be there to see it. You will be in Kravenstal, or Stellamere, or a small house in Thornfeld, watching the news and wondering whether the pain was worth the survival. You will wonder for the rest of your life. That is the cost of this kind of governance. You knew that when you took the job. Knowing it did not make it easier to carry.

You sided with the workers. Against the IMA, against the business class, against the international financial architecture that was strip-mining your country under the language of structural adjustment. The Khaled alliance became the defining political fact of the second half of your term. Together, you nationalized the industries the IMA wanted privatized. You imposed capital controls and wealth taxes. You told the international creditors that Veltria would pay its debts on Veltrian terms or not at all. The Orythians, seeing an opportunity, offered economic support without the IMA's conditions — not out of solidarity, but out of strategic interest. You accepted. You knew what you were accepting.

The economy did not boom. Revolutionary economies rarely do. But it stabilized in a different way than the IMA stabilization would have produced — workers kept their jobs, the state retained control of strategic industries, the social safety net expanded even as growth remained stagnant. The business community fled, taking their capital with them. You considered this an acceptable loss. Capital that requires inequality to function is capital the country can do without. That was the argument. It was not entirely wrong. It was also not entirely right. The truth, as always, was somewhere in the space the argument did not reach.

Internationally, Veltria became a symbol — of democratic socialism to its supporters, of creeping authoritarianism to its critics. The Arcturians imposed sanctions. The Orythians expanded their presence. You had traded dependency on one superpower for dependency on another. You told yourself the new dependency was less exploitative. You were not sure. You made the choice anyway because the alternative — IMA-administered immiseration — was worse. Choosing between bad options is most of what governance is. You had stopped pretending otherwise.

Liora became involved in the workers' movement — not as a journalist this time, but as an organizer. She had found her purpose in the same political tradition that had executed her grandfather. The irony was not lost on either of you. You talked about it once, late at night, after a political rally where she had spoken. She said: 'Grandfather died for a version of this. I'm living for a version of this. Those are different things.' You were not sure they were. You did not argue. Tomas found his way to the student movement — not the Ironborn, not the nationalists, but the young socialists who saw your government as insufficiently radical. Your children had become your left flank. You were, depending on the day, proud or terrified or both.

Jonas stayed. That surprised you. He said: 'I didn't sign up for revolutionary politics. I signed up for you. You're still you. The politics is just — context.' You wept. You had not wept since the inauguration. You had not let yourself. He held you while you wept, and the holding was a kind of governance too — the governance of a person who has decided that the political project and the personal project are the same project, and that both are worth finishing.

It happened on a Tuesday. The security detail had warned you about the specific threats — the Halvekist underground, the Tyvaren intelligence operatives, the lone actors radicalized by months of propaganda about your government. You had stopped reading the threat assessments around Week Thirty. There were too many. You could not govern while also tracking every person who wanted you dead. You delegated the tracking to the security services you had inherited, reformed, or retained from the Halvek years. They were competent. Competence is not the same as prevention. No security service can prevent every attack. The attacker only has to succeed once.

The funeral was a state occasion. The constitution you had fought for specified the succession procedures, and they were followed — the Speaker of Parliament assumed the acting Chancellorship, the election was scheduled, the institutions functioned as you had designed them to function. Your death became a test of the system you had built. The system passed. You were not there to see it.

In the days after, the country engaged in the collective exercise of memory that follows the death of a national figure. The newspapers ran retrospectives. The radio played your speeches. The parliament observed a moment of silence that stretched beyond the ceremonial into something genuine. The faction leaders who had opposed you issued statements of condolence that were sincere, strategic, or both. The international community sent representatives to the funeral — ambassadors, foreign ministers, the Arcturian Secretary of State. The Tyvaren government issued a statement denying involvement. Nobody believed them. Nobody could prove otherwise.

Your family received the country's grief with the particular composure of people who had been grieving you for months before you died. Jonas spoke at the funeral — brief, precise, the architect's mind finding structure in loss. He said: 'She believed that governance was a form of love. Not the soft kind. The hard kind — the kind that makes decisions knowing some of them will be wrong, that carries the weight of consequences, that keeps going when stopping would be easier. She loved this country the hard way. I loved her the hard way. I think she knew. I hope she knew.' Liora published your private papers — edited, annotated, contextualized. They became a bestseller and a historical document. Tomas did not speak publicly for a year. When he finally did, it was to announce a scholarship fund in your name for the children of public servants. He said: 'She would have wanted something useful.' He was right.

You did not live to see the country you built. You built it anyway. The foundation held. The institutions functioned. The election happened on schedule. The person who won — whoever they were, whatever they believed — governed under the system you created, with the powers you defined, constrained by the balances you designed. You were the first Chancellor of the Republic of Veltria. You were not the last. That is the legacy. That, and the children who survived you, and the husband who buried you, and the country that mourned you and kept going. Because you taught it, through fifty-two weeks of impossible decisions, that going forward is the only thing a country can do.

You resigned in Week Forty-Four. Not because you had lost a confidence vote, not because the military forced you out, not because the economic crisis made governance impossible — because Tomas needed you. Specifically, urgently, in a way that could not be delegated or rescheduled or fitted into the gaps between crisis meetings. He had stopped attending school entirely. The Ironborn had escalated from rhetoric to action — a bombing at a refugee center in Sevagrad, five dead, and Tomas's name on a list of youth members who had been brought in for questioning. He was not charged. He was not innocent. He was a fourteen-year-old boy who had been radicalized while you were governing.

You could not govern the country and save your son simultaneously. The country needed a Chancellor who could give it full attention. Your son needed a mother who could give him full attention. You chose your son. You announced your resignation in a national address that was the shortest speech you had ever given. You said: 'I was elected to protect the people of Veltria. The first people I am responsible for protecting are the ones in my own home. I have failed them. I am going to fix that. The country will be in good hands — I have built the institutions that will carry it forward. My children only have one mother. I am choosing them. I hope the country understands. Even if it doesn't, I am choosing them.'

The country understood more than you expected. The opinion polls showed approval for the decision. Parents wrote you letters — thousands of them — saying they would have made the same choice. The political class moved on quickly, as political classes do. A successor was elected within two months. The constitution continued to function. You had built a system that did not depend on you. The system worked. You watched it work from your home in Kravenstal, where Jonas had returned to his architecture practice and Liora was finishing her book and Tomas was in therapy, real therapy, the kind that takes years. He was getting better. Slowly. Genuinely. You were there to see it.

You never returned to politics. You wrote a memoir that was honest about the failures as well as the achievements. You gave lectures occasionally, at universities mostly, to students who had been children during your Chancellorship and wanted to understand what it had been like. You told them the truth: it had been the hardest thing you had ever done, and you had done it imperfectly, and you had left before the work was finished because some work is more important than governance. They asked if you regretted resigning. You said no. You said: 'My son is alive. He is healthy. He is going to be okay. I would trade every political achievement I ever made for that outcome, and I did, and I would do it again.'

Tomas graduated from university six years later. He studied psychology. He wanted to help children who had been through what he had been through. You attended the graduation. You wept. It was the best day of your life. It was worth the Chancellorship. It was worth everything.
